cells.tense: What they have is enough for the next step, and they are walking on it now.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to one person, which part is still unknown — then take today's step anyway, tonight, before the picture fills in.
cells.core:
Most of the middle is still missing from what you're carrying, and it isn't stopping you. You have enough to move, so you move, and you leave the far end unfinished while you do it. That's harder than it sounds, and most people don't manage it.

What this balance asks is smaller than it looks: name what you don't know yet, out loud, where someone can hear it. Not to solve it — to keep the line clear between what you've seen and what you're guessing. Then move. The step doesn't wait for the picture to fill in, and the picture won't fill in on its own anyway.
cells.sheetLine: You move without the whole picture, and don't wait for it.
cells.verb: going so deep into the pattern that thought meets its own floor
cells.place: where the next step is visible and the whole road is not

cells.tense: They will have settled every open question before they allow themselves to take the first step.
cells.ask: Write the three things you actually know about it, and act on one of them today — while the rest stays open.
cells.core:
When this works, the next step comes out of what you've already worked through. You see where a thing is heading, you take the one move that fits, and the rest stays open without threatening you — that's the ease most people don't get near.

Right now it's aimed the other way. Every open question gets turned over, compared, resolved ahead of time, and the resolving is what you do instead of the moving. The depth is real. It's just deep enough that you reach the point where no more thinking gets you further, and you keep going anyway. So do something smaller than the whole: write the three things you know, and act on one today. Leave the rest open. The pattern shows itself better once something has moved.
cells.sheetLine: You're finishing the picture before you'll allow the first step.

cells.tense: They knew a direction once, and they are still standing where the road ran out.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you did last week and why it mattered — out loud, in your own words, this week.
cells.core:
There's a way this goes when it's working: you act on the little you have, one step that makes sense, and you let the rest show itself as you go. That's enough to keep moving, and it usually is enough.

The next step hasn't shown up in a while, and you've been waiting for it. Not forcing anything, not pretending to be sure — just standing where you stopped, keeping your thinking to yourself until there's something worth saying. What's gone quiet isn't your thinking. It's the contact — someone hearing what you know. So tell one person one thing you did last week and why it mattered. Say it badly. The next step tends to arrive in company, not in the quiet, and you don't have to be sure of it to say it.
cells.sheetLine: Nothing to say until you're sure — and the not-saying outlasted the doubt.

cells.tense: They are already steering through the fog, and they keep calling it just getting through the week.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to one person, one thing you're figuring out as you go — and leave their answer out of it.
cells.core:
When this works, moving on partial light is something you do on purpose. You take the step you can see, you let the unclear part stay unclear, and you know that's what you're doing — not just getting by.

That part isn't named. You're the one making the calls while things are still unclear, and you talk about it like the week is doing it to you. Finding the way is real and steady, worked for, not a front. But you hand the credit to the situation. Say out loud, once, one thing you're figuring out as you go, and let the saying be enough for now. It tends to get steadier when the one doing the steering stops calling it fog.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering through this already. You keep calling it fog.
